title: Error Propagation & Significant Figures Rules
notes:
Significant Figures — Complete Rules

Rule 1: All non-zero digits (1-9) are always significant. Example: 3456 has 4 sig figs. Rule 2: Zeros between non-zero digits are significant. Example: 1003 has 4 sig figs; 201.5 has 4 sig figs. Rule 3: Leading zeros (zeros before the first non-zero digit) are NEVER significant. Example: 0.0045 has 2 sig figs; 0.000123 has 3 sig figs. These zeros only position the decimal point. Rule 4: Trailing zeros AFTER a decimal point ARE significant. Example: 2.500 has 4 sig figs; 0.07600 has 4 sig figs. Rule 5: Trailing zeros in a WHOLE NUMBER without a decimal point are AMBIGUOUS. Example: 3400 could have 2, 3, or 4 sig figs. Use scientific notation to clarify: 3.4 \times 10³ (2 sig figs), 3.40 \times 10³ (3 sig figs), 3.400 \times 10³ (4 sig figs).

Exact Numbers and Their Significant Figures

Exact numbers have NO uncertainty and therefore INFINITE significant figures. These include: (1) Counting numbers: 5 apples, 12 students — exact by definition. (2) Defined conversion factors: 1 m = 100 cm (exact), 1 inch = 2.54 cm (exact). (3) Mathematical constants in formulas: The 2 in KE = \frac{1}{2}mv², the 4 in sphere volume \frac{4}{3}\pi r³, the 2\pi in circumference 2\pi r. These do NOT limit the significant figures of the result. Only measured quantities limit precision.

Rules for Arithmetic Operations

Addition/Subtraction: The result must have the same number of decimal places as the measurement with the FEWEST decimal places. Example: 12.11 + 8.123 + 5.0 = 25.233 → 25.2 (1 decimal place, limited by 5.0). Multiplication/Division: The result must have the same number of significant figures as the measurement with the FEWEST significant figures. Example: 2.5 \times 3.42 = 8.55 → 8.6 (2 sig figs, limited by 2.5). Mixed operations: Apply each rule at each step, keeping one extra digit until the final answer, then round.

Round-off Rules

When rounding to a specific number of significant figures: (1) If the digit to be dropped is < 5, leave the preceding digit unchanged (4.34 → 4.3). (2) If the digit to be dropped is > 5, increase the preceding digit by 1 (4.36 → 4.4). (3) If the digit to be dropped is EXACTLY 5, use the 'round to even' rule: if the preceding digit is even, leave it; if odd, round up (4.35 → 4.4, 4.25 → 4.2). This minimizes systematic bias in repeated rounding. In NEB exams, standard rounding (5 rounds up) is generally accepted.

Error Propagation: Addition and Subtraction

For x = a \pm b: The maximum absolute error is \Delta x = \Delta a + \Delta b. Example: If A = (10.5 \pm 0.2) cm and B = (5.2 \pm 0.1) cm, then A + B = (15.7 \pm 0.3) cm and A - B = (5.3 \pm 0.3) cm. The absolute error is the SUM of individual absolute errors. This rule applies regardless of whether quantities are added or subtracted — errors always increase in these operations.

Error Propagation: Multiplication and Division

For x = a \times b or x = a/b: The maximum relative error is \frac{\Delta x}{x} = \frac{\Delta a}{a} + \frac{\Delta b}{b}. Example: Area A = l \times b where l = (10.5 \pm 0.2) cm and b = (5.2 \pm 0.1) cm. A = 54.6 cm². \frac{\Delta A}{A} = \frac{0.2}{10.5} + \frac{0.1}{5.2} = 0.0190 + 0.0192 = 0.0382. \Delta A = 0.0382 \times 54.6 = 2.08 \approx 2 cm². Answer: A = (55 \pm 2) cm² (rounded to match error precision).

Error Propagation: Powers and Roots

For x = a^n: The relative error is multiplied by the absolute value of the exponent: \frac{\Delta x}{x} = |n| \cdot \frac{\Delta a}{a}. Example: Volume of sphere V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r³. If r = (2.5 \pm 0.1) cm, then \frac{\Delta V}{V} = 3 \cdot \frac{0.1}{2.5} = 0.12 = 12%. V = 65.4 cm³, \Delta V = 7.8 cm³. Answer: V = (65 \pm 8) cm³. For square root (n = ½): \frac{\Delta x}{x} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta a}{a} — the relative error is HALVED. This is why taking square roots IMPROVES relative precision.

Combined Error Propagation (General Formula)

For a general expression Q = k \cdot a^p \cdot b^q \cdot c^r \cdots, the maximum fractional error is: \frac{\Delta Q}{Q} = |p|\frac{\Delta a}{a} + |q|\frac{\Delta b}{b} + |r|\frac{\Delta c}{c} + \cdots. The percentage error is this fraction times 100%. Example: Density \rho = m/(\frac{4}{3}\pi r³) = \frac{3m}{4\pi r³}. \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} = \frac{\Delta m}{m} + 3\frac{\Delta r}{r}. NEB strategy: Write the formula, identify all measured quantities and their exponents, then apply: add the percentage errors, each multiplied by its exponent's absolute value.

Practical Application: NEB Exam Pattern

In NEB exams, error propagation questions typically involve: (1) Density calculation from mass and volume (or diameter). (2) Acceleration due to gravity g = 4\pi²l/T² from pendulum experiment. (3) Resistivity \rho = RA/l from wire experiment. (4) Surface tension from capillary rise h = 2T/(\rho gr). The key steps are: compute the quantity, find the fractional error using the power rule, convert to absolute error, and report with proper significant figures. Always show the error formula substitution to earn full marks.
confusion: Leading zeros are NOT significant but trailing zeros AFTER a decimal ARE — 0.0045 has 2 sig figs (leading zeros are placeholders); 4.500 has 4 sig figs (trailing zeros after decimal indicate precision). The presence or absence of a decimal point is critical.

Multiplication uses sig figs; addition uses decimal places — These are DIFFERENT rules. 2.5 \times 3.42 = 8.6 (limited to 2 sig figs by 2.5). But 12.11 + 5.0 = 17.1 (limited to 1 decimal place by 5.0). Students often apply the wrong rule.

Scientific notation eliminates ambiguity about significant figures — 3400 is ambiguous (2, 3, or 4 sig figs); 3.400 \times 10³ clearly has 4 sig figs. Always use scientific notation when reporting results if there could be confusion about trailing zeros.

The 2 in \frac{1}{2}mv² is exact and does NOT limit sig figs — Only MEASURED quantities (m, v) have uncertainty. Mathematical constants (\pi, 2, 4/3) and exact conversion factors are treated as having infinite precision.

Percentage error in g from pendulum doubles the error in T — Since g = 4\pi²l/T², \frac{\Delta g}{g} = \frac{\Delta l}{l} + 2\frac{\Delta T}{T}. The factor of 2 comes from T being squared. This is why measuring the period of MANY oscillations (not just one) dramatically reduces the error in g.

Rounding the error determines how you round the result — If \Delta g = 0.69 m/s², round to 0.7 (1 sig fig in error). Then g = 9.87 must round to the same decimal place: 9.9. Report as (9.9 \pm 0.7) m/s², not (9.87 \pm 0.69).

Significant figures are about the INPUT precision, not the OUTPUT appearance — Reporting 8.55 when the inputs had only 2 sig figs falsely implies greater precision. Always round the FINAL answer to the appropriate number of sig figs, not intermediate calculations.

An error of 0 and a zero measurement are DIFFERENT — \Delta x = 0 means perfect measurement (impossible in practice); x = 0 means the quantity itself is zero. In error propagation, division by a measured quantity with small error can produce large relative error in the result.
practice: The side of a cube is measured as s = (2.5 \pm 0.1) cm. Find the volume, absolute error, and percentage error. [Solution: V = s³ = 15.625 cm³. \frac{\Delta V}{V} = 3\frac{\Delta s}{s} = 3 \times \frac{0.1}{2.5} = 0.12 = 12\%. \Delta V = 0.12 \times 15.625 = 1.875 \approx 1.9 cm³. Answer: V = (15.6 \pm 1.9) cm³ or (16 \pm 2) cm³ (using 1 sig fig in error).]

The length and breadth of a rectangle are l = (15.6 \pm 0.1) cm and b = (10.3 \pm 0.1) cm. Find area and its error. [Solution: A = l \times b = 160.68 cm². \frac{\Delta A}{A} = \frac{0.1}{15.6} + \frac{0.1}{10.3} = 0.00641 + 0.00971 = 0.01612. \Delta A = 0.01612 \times 160.68 = 2.59 \approx 2.6 cm². Answer: A = (161 \pm 3) cm².]

In a pendulum experiment, l = (100.0 \pm 0.1) cm and T = (2.00 \pm 0.02) s. Find g and its percentage error. [Solution: g = 4\pi²l/T² = 4(3.1416)²(1.00)/(2.00)² = 39.48/4.00 = 9.87 m/s². \frac{\Delta g}{g} = \frac{\Delta l}{l} + 2\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{0.1}{100.0} + 2\frac{0.02}{2.00} = 0.001 + 0.020 = 0.021 = 2.1\%. \Delta g = 0.021 \times 9.87 = 0.207 \approx 0.2 m/s². Answer: g = (9.87 \pm 0.21) m/s² \approx (9.9 \pm 0.2) m/s².]

The resistance of a wire is R = \rho l/A. Given \rho = (1.0 \pm 0.05) \times 10⁻⁶ \Omega\cdotm, l = (50.0 \pm 0.5) cm, A = (3.14 \pm 0.02) \times 10⁻⁷ m². Find R and its error. [Solution: R = \rho l/A = (1.0\times10⁻⁶)(0.50)/(3.14\times10⁻⁷) = 0.5\times10⁻⁶/3.14\times10⁻⁷ = 1.592 \Omega. \frac{\Delta R}{R} = \frac{0.05}{1.0} + \frac{0.5}{50.0} + \frac{0.02}{3.14} = 0.05 + 0.01 + 0.00637 = 0.0664. \Delta R = 0.0664 \times 1.592 = 0.106 \approx 0.1 \Omega. Answer: R = (1.59 \pm 0.11) \Omega.]

Five students measure a length: 10.2, 10.4, 10.1, 10.3, 10.5 cm. Find mean, mean absolute error, relative error, and percentage error. [Solution: Mean = (10.2+10.4+10.1+10.3+10.5)/5 = 51.5/5 = 10.30 cm. Absolute errors: 0.10, 0.10, 0.20, 0.00, 0.20. Mean abs error = 0.60/5 = 0.12 \approx 0.1 cm. Relative error = 0.12/10.30 = 0.0117. Percentage error = 1.17% \approx 1.2%. Answer: l = (10.3 \pm 0.1) cm, 1% error.]

The focal length of a lens is f = 10.0 \pm 0.2 cm. Find the power of the lens and its error. [Solution: P = 1/f = 1/0.10 = 10.0 D. \frac{\Delta P}{P} = \frac{\Delta f}{f} = \frac{0.2}{10.0} = 0.02 = 2\% (since P \propto f⁻¹). \Delta P = 0.02 \times 10.0 = 0.2 D. Answer: P = (10.0 \pm 0.2) D.]

The pressure P of a gas is related to volume V by PV = constant. If V = (2.0 \pm 0.1) L and P = (3.0 \pm 0.2) atm, check if PV is consistent and find the percentage error in the product. [Solution: PV = 6.0 L\cdotatm. \frac{\Delta(PV)}{PV} = \frac{\Delta P}{P} + \frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{0.2}{3.0} + \frac{0.1}{2.0} = 0.0667 + 0.05 = 0.1167 = 11.7\%. \Delta(PV) = 0.1167 \times 6.0 = 0.7 \approx 0.7 L\cdotatm. Answer: PV = (6.0 \pm 0.7) L\cdotatm.]

The kinetic energy of a 2.0 kg object moving at 3.0 m/s is KE = \frac{1}{2}mv². If the mass has 5% error and velocity has 3% error, find KE and its percentage error. [Solution: KE = 0.5 \times 2.0 \times 9.0 = 9.0 J. \frac{\Delta KE}{KE} = \frac{\Delta m}{m} + 2\frac{\Delta v}{v} = 5\% + 2(3\%) = 11\%. \Delta KE = 0.11 \times 9.0 = 0.99 \approx 1.0 J. Answer: KE = (9.0 \pm 1.0) J.]

A sphere has radius r = (1.0 \pm 0.1) cm. Find its surface area and percentage error. [Solution: A = 4\pi r² = 4\pi(1.0)² = 12.57 cm². \frac{\Delta A}{A} = 2\frac{\Delta r}{r} = 2 \times \frac{0.1}{1.0} = 0.20 = 20\%. \Delta A = 0.20 \times 12.57 = 2.51 \approx 2.5 cm². Answer: A = (12.6 \pm 2.5) cm². The large error (20%) shows why precise radius measurement matters for area calculations.]

The time period of a vibrating tuning fork is T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} where m = (0.500 \pm 0.005) kg and k = (200 \pm 5) N/m. Find T and its percentage error. [Solution: T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.500/200} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.0025} = 2\pi(0.05) = 0.314 s. \frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta m}{m} + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta k}{k} = \frac{1}{2}(\frac{0.005}{0.500}) + \frac{1}{2}(\frac{5}{200}) = 0.005 + 0.0125 = 0.0175 = 1.75\%. \Delta T = 0.0175 \times 0.314 = 0.0055 \approx 0.006 s. Answer: T = (0.314 \pm 0.006) s.]
universalFacts: The convention of rounding 5 to the nearest even number (round-half-to-even) was adopted internationally in 2019 (IEEE 754 standard) — This reduces systematic bias: if you always round 5 up, over many calculations you'll consistently overestimate. Round-to-even balances this by rounding 2.5 to 2 and 3.5 to 4.

NEB exam tip: In pendulum experiments, timing 20 oscillations and dividing by 20 reduces the human reaction time error by a factor of \sqrt{20} \approx 4.5 compared to timing 1 oscillation — This is why lab manuals always ask for multiple oscillations; it's the single most effective way to improve g measurement.

The rule that relative errors add for multiplication comes from logarithmic differentiation — Taking ln of Q = ab gives ln Q = ln a + ln b; differentiating yields dQ/Q = da/a + db/b. This mathematical fact underlies ALL error propagation for products and quotients.

In experimental physics, the 'weakest link' determines overall precision — If one measurement has 10% error and another has 1%, the result is dominated by the 10% error. To improve overall precision, focus on the LEAST precise measurement first; improving the already-precise one wastes effort.

The uncertainty principle \Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq \hbar/2 sets a FUNDAMENTAL limit on precision — No matter how good your instruments, you cannot simultaneously know position and momentum with arbitrary precision. This is not an experimental limitation but a property of nature itself.

Historically, the precision of navigation depended on timekeeping accuracy — John Harrison's marine chronometer (1761) reduced longitude error from hundreds of kilometers to a few kilometers, solving the centuries-old 'longitude problem' and revolutionizing global trade and exploration.

The concept of 'significant figures' was developed in the context of logarithmic tables and slide rules — Before calculators, scientists used logarithm tables where numbers were written with 4-7 significant figures. The rules of sig figs evolved to match the precision of these computational tools.
